scenes.name: the four rungs and their scope
scenes.visual: A physical hierarchy diagram showing the four rungs of storage, nested by physical scope: registers and SRAM inside each multiprocessor, L2 cache spanning the die, and HBM stacks sitting off-die on the package. Callouts detail capacity and access scope.

beats.say: The hardware organizes memory into four rungs: registers, L one and shared memory, the L two cache, and H B M.
beats.show: A four-rung vertical ladder illuminates: bottom rung in coral 'HBM · 80 GB', middle rungs in teal 'L2 · 50 MB' and 'L1 & Shared · 256 KB', top rung in blue 'Registers · 256 KB'.

beats.say: Counted across the whole chip, the registers hold thirty-four point six megabytes, while H B M holds eighty gigabytes: about twenty-five hundred times as much.
beats.show: Capacities multiply across all 132 SMs: Registers = 34.6 MB, L1/Shared = 34.6 MB, L2 = 52.4 MB, HBM = 80 GB (a 2,500× span on a log scale).

beats.say: Each rung is also defined by scope: who is allowed to see it. Registers belong to a single thread and nobody else.
beats.show: A boundary card highlights: 'Scope: Registers = 1 private thread'.

beats.say: Shared memory is seen by all threads in one block. The L two cache is seen by all multiprocessors. H B M is seen by everything, including other chips.
beats.show: Expanding scope boundaries animate: Shared memory = 1 block; L2 = 132 SMs; HBM = entire package and system. Takeaway: 'to exchange data, threads must meet at a level they both see'.

scenes.name: less than a thousandth of the model
scenes.visual: A 2D area comparison drawn strictly to scale. A huge square represents the 140 gigabytes of a 70B model. Inside it, a tiny square representing all fast on-chip memory combined (121.6 megabytes) accounts for less than one-tenth of one percent.

beats.say: Sum up every single byte of fast storage on the chip: all the registers, all the shared memory, and the entire L two cache.
beats.show: A tally card aggregates on-chip storage: '34.6 MB registers + 34.6 MB L1/shared + 52.4 MB L2 = 121.6 megabytes total'.

beats.say: Together, they hold one hundred and twenty-one point six megabytes. A seventy-billion-parameter model takes a hundred and forty gigabytes.
beats.show: A massive 140 GB square draws across the screen. Beside it, the 121.6 MB on-chip total is placed to scale as a tiny square in the corner.

beats.say: All the fast memory on the chip holds less than a thousandth of the model: zero point zero eight seven percent.
beats.show: A dimension bracket highlights the ratio: 'on-chip fast memory = 0.087% of the model (under 1/1,000th)'. The L2 alone holds only one part in twenty-six hundred.

beats.say: Generating a token reads every weight once, so by the time a weight could be reused, thousands of others have evicted it. Every token's weights must come up from H B M.
beats.show: An eviction animation shows cache lines constantly overwriting each other. Takeaway: 'there is nowhere on-chip to keep the weights: each token must stream the entire model from HBM'.

scenes.name: latencies and bandwidths on the ladder
scenes.visual: Dual horizontal log-axis charts for all four rungs. Top chart: latency in clock ticks (1 tick -> 29 -> 41 -> 263 -> 479 ticks). Bottom chart: bandwidth per multiprocessor per tick (1,536 bytes -> 128 -> 39 -> 12.8 bytes).

beats.say: Measured on real hardware, latency climbs steeply with every step down the ladder.
beats.show: A latency chart plots values in ticks: 'Registers: 1 tick', 'Shared memory: 29 ticks', 'L1 cache: 41 ticks', 'L2 cache: 263 ticks', 'HBM: 479 ticks'.

beats.say: Bandwidth falls just as fast in the other direction.
beats.show: A bandwidth chart plots bytes per SM per tick: 'Registers: 1,536 bytes', 'Shared memory: 128 bytes', 'L2: 39 bytes', 'HBM: 12.8 bytes'.

beats.say: Top to bottom, latency grows nearly five hundred times, while bandwidth drops a hundred and twenty times.
beats.show: Two comparative ratio arrows span the charts: latency grows 479×; bandwidth falls 120×.

beats.say: Reaching down to H B M for a byte is vastly more expensive than computing on a byte already at the top. G P U programming is the craft of staging data upward.
beats.show: A graphic shows data tiles moving upward from HBM into shared memory and registers, keeping the amber math units operating at peak. Takeaway pill: 'latency grows 500× and bandwidth drops 120×: stage data upward'.

checks.claim: All on-chip memory: 34.6 MB registers + 34.6 MB L1/shared + 52.4 MB L2 = 121.63 MB, which is 0.0869% of 140 GB, quoted as '121.6 megabytes' and '0.087 percent'
L2 cache share: 140 GB / 52.4288 MB = 2,670.28, quoted as 'one part in twenty-six hundred'
Latency ratio HBM to registers: 478.8 / 1 = 478.8x, quoted as 'nearly five hundred times'
Bandwidth ratio registers to HBM: 1,536 / 12.8 = 120.0x, quoted as 'a hundred and twenty times'
